rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the closing section resumes the sūrah’s opening topic; its apparent distance from that topic masks a coherent discourse.
rows.anchor: This last section of the sūrah, as referred to earlier is linked to the topic discussed at the beginning of the sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening refutation shifted at verse 11 to threaten and admonish Quraysh and reassure the Prophet; the repeated opening word at verse 149 resumes that subject.
rows.anchor: the discourse from verse eleven onwards digressed to threaten and admonish the Quraysh and to assure the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to ask angel worshippers why they assign daughters to God when they choose sons for themselves; attributing children is ignorant, and their choice is still more absurd.
rows.anchor: if they choose sons for themselves, why do choose daughters for their Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human intellect and nature should ascribe only fitting traits to God; the idolaters instead assign Him a trait they themselves consider shameful.
rows.anchor: the requisite of human intellect and nature that they should have ascribed to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question challenges their basis for calling angels God’s daughters: did they witness the angels’ creation? Islahi links the challenge to the parallel in Sūrah Zukhruf.
rows.anchor: Did they witness the creation of angels by God?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They have no intellectual, scriptural, or visual proof for claiming that God has children; they fabricate the claim and are liars.
rows.anchor: neither have an intellectual argument nor any scriptural support to back their claim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God wanted children and could have sons, there is no reason He would prefer daughters or accept what idolaters themselves reject unless compelled.
rows.anchor: why would he prefer daughters to sons? If He was also capable of producing sons why did He tolerate something which the Idolaters were not ready to put up with unless compelled to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their firm judgment shows that their intellect has gone wrong.
rows.anchor: what has gone wrong with their intellect that they make such a firm and inalterable decision

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their willingness to choose for God what they reject for themselves shows irrationality; grasping this requires only a little heed, not elaborate reasoning.
rows.anchor: this thing is not something which even requires any reasoning; it only requires paying slight heed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A clear proof means a divine book: anyone making a claim about God must produce scriptural evidence, and His revealed Book is the clearest proof.
rows.anchor: the clearest of such arguments is His Book which He has revealed for the guidance of His people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads the exaltation in verse 159 as a parenthetical interruption and verse 160 as an exception linked back to verse 158, inserted to reject a horrific attribution immediately.
rows.anchor: is a parenthetical sentence and the verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people associate angels with God’s being and jinn with His rights and attributes, despite God alone deserving worship.
rows.anchor: they made the angels as partners in the being of God and made the jinn partners in the rights and attributes of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They wrongly believe jinn can harm or benefit people and reveal the unseen, then worship them and offer sacrifices and vows.
rows.anchor: regard the jinn to have the authority to harm and benefit people and to be a means of finding out the matters of the unseen world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn know they are God’s creatures and will face accountability; their sinful members will be punished, though people foolishly worship them as partners.
rows.anchor: the jinn themselves are fully convinced that they are creatures of God and they shall one day be held accountable before Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The immediate glorification rejects the detestable association: God is exalted above every such attribution, has no partner in being or attributes, and alone owns the rights due to Him.
rows.anchor: the exalted person of God is above all such ascriptions; neither is anyone a partner in His being nor His attributes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception to the jinn being brought before God means that those whom God guides as worthy under His established practice are spared arrest and protected from Satan’s lures.
rows.anchor: only those will be saved from this arrest whom the Almighty according to His established practice guides to the right path

rows.speaker: Zamaksharī
rows.claim: Zamaksharī concludes that the jinn mentioned here are angels.
rows.anchor: It beats me what led Zamaksharī349 to conclude that the jinn referred to here are angels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects identifying jinn with angels because the Qur’ān treats them as distinct creations with different traits; jinn are only closer to angels than humans in created substance, being made of fire rather than light or clay.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān mentions angels and jinn as two distinct creations having different traits from one another. There is no possibility of regarding them to be one.

rows.speaker: some exegetes
rows.claim: Some exegetes read عليه as ‘against’ God, with God as the pronoun’s antecedent; Islahi is unconvinced, though on this reading only people destined for Hell can be lured by jinn and their worshippers.
rows.anchor: some exegetes351 have interpreted the word ْيَلَع to means “against”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading echoes God’s answer to Satan: only those who follow Satan can be led astray, while divine trials test people and do not harm those of God’s servants who try to pass.
rows.anchor: the trials which the Almighty makes people pass through are not meant to lead them astray; they are only meant to test them

rows.speaker: Imām H @amīd al-Dīn Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī takes the antecedent of the genitive pronoun as ‘what you worship’; the verse then means people can induce worship of these deities only among those who intend to enter Hell.
rows.anchor: the antecedent of the genitive pronoun is اَمَو َونُدُبْعَت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says he is not fully convinced by Farāhī’s interpretation and records it only for readers to consider.
rows.anchor: I am not fully convinced of this interpretation. I have only referred to it so that it can remain in the notice of those who want to reflect on these verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel speaks at God’s command to explain his own status and that of all angels, exposing angel worshippers by testimony from the angels themselves.
rows.anchor: archangel Gabriel, at the behest of the Almighty, explains his own status and that of all the angels before God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’ān sometimes puts words directly in Gabriel’s mouth when that is more eloquent; Maryam 64–65 is an example, and the angels’ own testimony is the strongest rebuttal here.
rows.anchor: there are a number of places in the Qur’ān where during a discourse something is said directly through the tongue of Gabriel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every angel has a prescribed, limited sphere of authority; angels are submissive workers who cannot exceed their limits, act without God’s permission, or save worshippers from punishment.
rows.anchor: the circle of activity of every angel is prescribed and they have limited access

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels stand in rows and glorify God; Islahi links this to the prayer around the Throne, called dhikr at the sūrah’s opening and tasbīḥ here.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, this is an allusion to the prayer of the angels around the throne of the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasbīḥ means absolving God of notions and attributions beneath His majesty; angels thereby deny all negative attributions, especially partnership with God.
rows.anchor: The dominant meaning of حٌْیِبْسَت is to absolve God from all concepts and ascriptions that are against and beyond His majesty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Quraysh heard that Jews and other nations rejected messengers, they mocked and claimed that, if given earlier teaching or a messenger, they would follow and become God’s chosen servants.
rows.anchor: They would say that had the teaching of the earlier people come to them or had a messenger of God come to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People lacking an opportunity often promise great deeds if given power, then fail when tested; Islahi illustrates this with people claiming they would restore ʿUmar’s rule but becoming failures, embezzlers, or thieves.
rows.anchor: had he been blessed with that thing he would have accomplished great feats; however, when he actually receives that thing more often than not he becomes a worse failure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once the teaching they wanted came, Quraysh rejected it, made excuses, and would soon learn the consequence of their denial.
rows.anchor: when the thing these people were

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses warn Quraysh that if they do not reform, they will face the established fate of earlier rejecters of God’s messengers.
rows.anchor: the purpose is to warn the Quraysh: if they do not mend their ways then the same established practice of God will materialize for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word kalimah refers to God’s established practice concerning His messengers, also stated in Qur’ān 58:20–21 and 40:51.
rows.anchor: The word َمِلَكةُ refers to the established practice of the Almighty which relates to His messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A people who reject truth after a messenger conclusively conveys it are destroyed; the messenger is like a court of justice, and the ensuing struggle ends with the messenger and companions prevailing over their foes.
rows.anchor: A messenger is the final means of communicating the truth to his people; for this reason, his status is that of a court of justice for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reminds readers to distinguish a nabī from a rasūl, a distinction he says he has explained elsewhere in the exegesis.
rows.anchor: Here, the difference between a nabī (prophet) and a rasūl (messenger) should also be kept in mind by the readers
